text: Drop Mount Everest into the deepest part of the ocean, and its peak would still be over a mile underwater. Let's go down.
The ocean holds ninety-nine percent of Earth's living space. As one bathtub, it would be eleven hundred kilometres on each side. Good luck finding the plug.
Here's you, for scale. And a blue whale, the biggest animal on Earth. It usually hunts about a hundred metres down, in the sunlit zone.
Two hundred and ten metres. USS Triton's diving depth. In 1960, it became the first submarine to circle the world underwater.
Two hundred and fifty-three metres. The deepest free dive ever, on one breath. The pressure is twenty-six times the surface. Enough to crush most human lungs.
Whales don't mind. Blue whales reach about five hundred metres. Sperm whales go far deeper, hunting giant squid.
Seven hundred and thirty metres. The danger zone for attack submarines. Any deeper, and the hull could implode.
Take the Burj Khalifa, the world's tallest building, and hang it upside down from the surface. Its tip stops about here.
One thousand metres. No more sunlight. Welcome to the midnight zone.
Many animals here skip eyes altogether, like these eyeless shrimp around underwater volcanoes. The water is barely above freezing, but near the vents it can top four hundred degrees.
Almost three thousand metres. The deepest dive by any mammal: Cuvier's beaked whale. It has also held its breath for over three hours. Show off.
Even it can't reach the Titanic, three thousand eight hundred metres down. The pressure here is three hundred and eighty times what you feel right now.
Yet things still live here. Fangtooth fish. Hagfish. And the dumbo octopus, the deepest living octopus.
Six thousand metres. The hadal zone: the ocean's deepest trenches, like the Mariana Trench.
Eight thousand three hundred metres. The deepest fish ever filmed, a little snailfish.
Tip Mount Everest into the trench, and the summit stops about here. Still not the bottom.
In 2012, director James Cameron dived solo nearly eleven kilometres down, in his Deepsea Challenger.
But the record went to Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh, back in 1960. They reached Challenger Deep, the lowest point on Earth, almost eleven thousand metres down.
Robots followed. Japan's Kaiko collected three hundred and fifty species from the deep sea floor, between 1995 and 2003. And since 2019, over twenty people have touched the bottom.
Yet we've explored only five to ten percent of the ocean. There could be thousands of species down here we've never met.
We've only just begun to understand the dark world beneath us. So next time you're at the beach, maybe don't look down.
